share.who: a DBA or backend engineer tuning how long PostgreSQL takes to recover after a crash
share.why: shorter checkpoint intervals buy faster crash recovery at the price of more dirty-page flushing: a tuning rule worth saving

replay.twist: The hook asks why a COMMIT flushes only 1 file and not your table. On a second watch the last line answers it as a lesson: only the WAL file is flushed at COMMIT, and the checkpoint plus the REDO replay are what keep your table safe.

length_reason: About 90 s on purpose: one mechanism with four stages (WAL record, flush at COMMIT, checkpoint, REDO), each with a real default, setting, function or file name from the PostgreSQL 18 docs, plus the checkpoint trade-off and the synchronous_commit catch.

claims.say: Why does a PostgreSQL COMMIT flush 1 file, not your table?
claims.quote: Using WAL results in a significantly reduced number of disk writes, because only the WAL file needs to be flushed to disk to guarantee that a transaction is committed, rather than every data file changed by the transaction.

claims.say: The answer is the write-ahead log, WAL: changes to data files must be written only after those changes have been logged.
claims.quote: WAL's central concept is that changes to data files (where tables and indexes reside) must be written only after those changes have been logged, that is, after WAL records describing the changes have been flushed to permanent storage.

claims.say: The path has a WAL record, a flush at COMMIT, a checkpoint, and REDO after a crash.
claims.quote: At checkpoint time, all dirty data pages are flushed to disk and a special checkpoint record is written to the WAL file. In the event of a crash, the crash recovery procedure looks at the latest checkpoint record to determine the point in the WAL (known as the redo record) from which it should start the REDO operation.

claims.say: Each change is appended to the WAL at an insert position called the Log Sequence Number, a byte offset that only increases.
claims.quote: WAL records are appended to the WAL files as each new record is written. The insert position is described by a Log Sequence Number (LSN) that is a byte offset into the WAL, increasing monotonically with each new record.

claims.say: WAL files live in pg_wal, normally 16 MB each, named in ever-increasing numbers; the first is 000000010000000000000001.
claims.quote: WAL files are stored in the directory pg_wal under the data directory, as a set of segment files, normally each 16 MB in size (but the size can be changed by altering the --wal-segsize initdb option). Segment files are given ever-increasing numbers as names, starting at 000000010000000000000001.

claims.say: If your 1 changed table page is still only in memory, would a crash lose it? (answered by REDO)
claims.quote: we do not need to flush data pages to disk on every transaction commit, because we know that in the event of a crash we will be able to recover the database using the log: any changes that have not been applied to the data pages can be redone from the WAL records.

claims.say: Second, the flush. At COMMIT, only the WAL file has to be flushed to disk, not every data file the transaction changed. That means significantly fewer disk writes.
claims.quote: Using WAL results in a significantly reduced number of disk writes, because only the WAL file needs to be flushed to disk to guarantee that a transaction is committed, rather than every data file changed by the transaction.

claims.say: synchronous_commit is on by default (terminal line).
claims.quote: Valid values are remote_apply, on (the default), remote_write, local, and off.

claims.say: pg_current_wal_flush_lsn: last location known to be written to durable storage (terminal line).
claims.quote: pg_current_wal_flush_lsn displays the current write-ahead log flush location. The insertion location is the "logical" end of the write-ahead log at any instant, while the write location is the end of what has actually been written out from the server's internal buffers, and the flush location is the last location known to be written to durable storage.

claims.say: At checkpoint time, all dirty data pages are flushed to disk and a checkpoint record is written to the WAL.
claims.quote: At checkpoint time, all dirty data pages are flushed to disk and a special checkpoint record is written to the WAL file.

claims.say: The CHECKPOINT command forces one (an immediate checkpoint).
claims.quote: The CHECKPOINT command forces an immediate checkpoint when the command is issued, without waiting for a regular checkpoint scheduled by the system

claims.say: A checkpoint begins every checkpoint_timeout, 5 minutes by default, or when max_wal_size, 1 GB by default, is about to be exceeded.
claims.quote: A checkpoint is begun every checkpoint_timeout seconds, or if max_wal_size is about to be exceeded, whichever comes first. The default settings are 5 minutes and 1 GB, respectively.

claims.say: checkpoint_timeout default 5min (on-screen value).
claims.quote: The default is five minutes (5min).

claims.say: max_wal_size default 1GB (on-screen value).
claims.quote: The default is 1 GB.

claims.say: Fourth, REDO: no, the page is not lost. After a crash, PostgreSQL reads the latest checkpoint record to find the redo record, and redoes the changes from that point in the WAL.
claims.quote: In the event of a crash, the crash recovery procedure looks at the latest checkpoint record to determine the point in the WAL (known as the redo record) from which it should start the REDO operation. any changes that have not been applied to the data pages can be redone from the WAL records.

claims.say: Shorter checkpoint intervals mean faster crash recovery, but dirty data pages are flushed more often.
claims.quote: Reducing checkpoint_timeout and/or max_wal_size causes checkpoints to occur more often. This allows faster after-crash recovery, since less work will need to be redone. However, one must balance this against the increased cost of flushing dirty data pages more often.

claims.say: With synchronous_commit off, COMMIT does not wait for the flush; a crash can lose recent transactions, for up to three times wal_writer_delay; the database stays consistent.
claims.quote: In off mode, there is no waiting, so there can be a delay between when success is reported to the client and when the transaction is later guaranteed to be safe against a server crash. (The maximum delay is three times wal_writer_delay.) Unlike fsync, setting this parameter to off does not create any risk of database inconsistency: an operating system or database crash might result in some recent allegedly-committed transactions being lost, but the database state will be just the same as if those transactions had been aborted cleanly.

claims.say: The actual maximum duration of the risk window is three times wal_writer_delay; risk is data loss, not corruption.
claims.quote: The actual maximum duration of the risk window is three times wal_writer_delay because the WAL writer is designed to favor writing whole pages at a time during busy periods. The risk that is taken by using asynchronous commit is of data loss, not data corruption.

claims.say: wal_writer_delay default is 200 milliseconds (200ms).
claims.quote: The default value is 200 milliseconds (200ms).

claims.say: So a COMMIT flushes only the WAL file; the checkpoint and the REDO replay keep your table safe.
claims.quote: only the WAL file needs to be flushed to disk to guarantee that a transaction is committed, rather than every data file changed by the transaction. At checkpoint time, all dirty data pages are flushed to disk and a special checkpoint record is written to the WAL file.
